newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia polls will bolster ethnic purity, say Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia polls will bolster ethnic purity, say Serbs.

text.p: Most Bosnian Serbs in Doboj, from which thousands of Moslems were expelled in 1992, hope Saturday's election, when some Moslems briefly returned to vote, will only strengthen their republic and its ethnic purity.

"I expect that after these elections the Serb Republic will become a real state. The Moslems would do better to stay where they are. People here wouldn't like them to return," said Milan, a waiter from Doboj.

The Serb Republic is a separate entity in Bosnia carved out during the war, covering roughly half of the country. The other half is the Croat-Moslem Federation. People in both parts voted on Saturday for a three-member presidency, parliament and separate national assemblies.
"If they return the question is -- why on earth did we fight for four years?" said Milan.
Bosnia's first post-war election, envisaged by last November's Dayton peace treaty, generally passed without incident, under tight security and international supervision.
But observers believe the Serb, Croat and Moslem nationalist parties will sweep a clear victory in their respective territories, which will only underline the country's ethnic partition.
Some 700 Doboj Moslems living in exile crossed ceasefire lines on Saturday to cast their vote, many of them hoping to get a glimpse of their old homes. The Serbs largely ignored former neighbours.
"They didn't come here to vote but just to be back in town. They hope they will creep back in time and regain their homes. But there is no way it will happen," Milan said.

Doboj had a pre-war Moslem majority of some 40,000 with around 30,000 Serbs. After Serb militia captured the town and the whole of northern Bosnia, less than 1,000 Moslems remained in town. Others were brutally expelled to government-controlled areas.
An estimated 19,000 Serbs were brought into Doboj by bus from across Bosnia and Serbia to vote on Saturday.
"They should stay and live where they are and we should live on our own, here. Maybe eventually we'll become good neighbours," said Milan.

U.S. diplomats and other architects of the Dayton peace treaty, which envisaged the elections, hope the voting will create democratic structures that will eventually overpower nationalist tendencies and help unify the country.
But Doboj Serbs do not share their hopes.

"I didn't want things to be like this in the first place. But...why should we reunite with the Moslems? We fought to have our own Serb state," said Ranko, 22, who spent three years in the Bosnian Serb army.

"Moslems can return here but sooner or later we'll have trouble -- someone will provoke someone else and the incident will grow into a conflict. Don't forget so many people have lost houses or family members in the war," he said.
